title: The JVP rule of `clamp` returns zero for `max` where `x <= max < min`, where the result is `max`
description: `lax.clamp(min, x, max)` lowers to StableHLO `clamp`, which is `minimum(maximum(x, min), max)`.
So where `min > max` the result is `max` for every `x`,
and near a point with `x < max < min` it is the function `max` alone, with derivative 1 in `max`.
The rule for `min` guards against `min > max` with `lt(min, max)`, so it returns 0 there, which is right.
The rule for `max`, `select(lt(max, operand), g, _zeros(operand))`, has no such guard:
it returns the tangent of `max` only where `max < x`, so where `x < max < min` it returns 0 too.
Every rule returns 0, and forward and reverse mode compute a zero derivative.
`jnp.clip`, which is written with `max` and `min`, gets the derivative right.
`Jax.Lax.clampJvp_correct` proves the three rules correct where, in every entry,
`x > max`, or `min < x < max`, or `x < min < max`.
At every other point where `clamp` is differentiable, some entry has `x <= max < min`, and the rules are wrong there.
The docstring of `lax.clamp` gives `min` where `x < min`, which disagrees with what XLA computes where `min > max`.
reproducer: # XLA computes minimum(maximum(x, lo), hi), so with lo > hi the result is hi, also near the point.
print(lax.clamp(lo, x, hi - 1e-3), lax.clamp(lo, x, hi + 1e-3))
# So the derivative is 1 in hi and 0 in x and lo, as jnp.clip computes.
# The rule of lax.clamp for hi returns 0, because hi < x is false.
# The same at x = hi < lo, where the result is hi too.
